nameStory: The Shag-rug Nudibranch gets its quirky name from the countless finger-like projections called cerata that cover its back, creating a texture remarkably similar to a shaggy carpet or rug. These fuzzy-looking appendages give this sea slug its distinctive "hairy" appearance that's impossible to miss underwater.
description: The Shag-rug Nudibranch is a soft-bodied sea slug that crawls along rocky surfaces in shallow ocean waters. Its most striking feature is the dense carpet of finger-like projections covering its back, giving it a fuzzy, almost furry appearance. These nudibranchs are typically grayish in color and can grow to about 4 inches long. Like all nudibranchs, they're shell-less marine snails that breathe through their skin and external gills.

idTips.label: Cerata covering
idTips.description: Dense carpet of finger-like projections (cerata) covers the entire back, feeling soft and squishy to gentle touch, creating an unmistakable shag-rug texture

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Overall grayish coloration with subtle variations from pale gray to darker gray-brown, often with translucent quality that reveals internal structures

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Elongated, flattened body that tapers toward the tail, with a distinct head bearing two prominent horn-like tentacles (rhinophores)

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Adults typically reach 2-4 inches in length, making them one of the larger nudibranchs you'll encounter in New England waters

idTips.label: Movement style
idTips.description: Glides smoothly across surfaces using its muscular foot, leaving a slight slime trail, and can gently wave its cerata when disturbed

habitat: Look for Shag-rug Nudibranchs in shallow rocky intertidal zones and subtidal areas along New England's coast, especially around tide pools and kelp beds. They prefer areas with good water circulation where sea anemones are abundant, as these are their primary food source. You'll most commonly spot them during low tide on rock faces, under ledges, or among seaweed at depths from the low tide line down to about 100 feet.

seasonality.spring: Active feeding season begins as water temperatures rise, making this an excellent time to spot them during low tides. Look for them grazing on sea anemones in tide pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily found during daylight low tides. This is also their breeding season, so you might see them in pairs or small groups.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper waters. Continue looking in the same rocky intertidal habitats, though they may be less abundant in the shallowest areas.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and typically found in deeper, more protected waters. Rarely seen during winter tide pooling, though they don't completely disappear from shallow areas.

funFact: This nudibranch is essentially a solar-powered predator that steals the stinging cells from sea anemones it eats and stores them in the tips of its fuzzy projections, turning itself into a living weapon powered by recycled sea anemone venom!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other gray nudibranchs, but no other New England species has such a dense, uniform covering of finger-like projections. Remember: if it looks like a fuzzy gray carpet with tentacles, it's a Shag-rug Nudibranch.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "nudibranch" literally means "naked gills," referring to the external breathing structures these sea slugs carry. Despite their delicate appearance, nudibranchs are actually highly specialized predators that have evolved to eat specific prey items.
compareHints: As the only Aeolidia species in New England waters, the Shag-rug Nudibranch is most similar to other aeolid nudibranchs in the region, but none have such densely packed cerata covering the entire back. Other aeolids typically have their finger-like projections arranged in distinct clusters or rows, while the Shag-rug's cerata form a continuous fuzzy carpet. The uniform grayish coloration also helps distinguish it from more colorful nudibranch species.
